title: The Autumn Evan Williams Bought Odeo Back From Its Investors
dek: In 2006 the head of a fading podcasting start-up told his investors it was going nowhere, offered them their money back, and kept a side project called Twitter.

story.founder: Evan Williams, Biz Stone, Jack Dorsey
story.event: Giving up on podcasting and buying Odeo back from its investors
story.summary: In September 2006 Evan Williams, chief executive of the venture-backed podcasting start-up Odeo, wrote to its investors that the company was going nowhere and offered to buy back their shares so they would not lose money. On 25 October 2006 his self-funded Obvious Corp announced it had bought all of Odeo's assets, including the young Twitter service. Twitter took off in 2007; some investors later questioned how much he had known about its prospects.
paragraphs: One day in September 2006, Evan Williams, chief executive of the San Francisco podcasting start-up Odeo, wrote to its investors. According to Business Insider, which later reported the letter, he told them the company was going nowhere, that he felt bad about it, and that he wanted to buy back their shares so they would not take a loss.

Odeo had raised $5 million, led by Charles River Ventures, and launched in 2005; a year on, TechCrunch noted, it faced dozens of rivals, including Apple's iTunes. Williams had already admitted mistakes in public: not focusing the product, building for other people, raising too much money too soon. Odeo still had plenty of money in the bank and could have held out for a couple of years, he wrote, but "Just because we could spend the money doesn't mean we should." There was also a side project, Twitter, built from Jack Dorsey's idea of sharing what you were doing by text message. In the letter Williams called it one of the pieces of value in Odeo, but "much too early to tell what's there", with fewer than 5,000 registered users. An engineer recalled a summer meeting about switching it off.

The investors agreed. On 25 October 2006 Williams announced that Obvious Corp, a company he had started with help from Biz Stone and other Odeo staff and funded himself, had bought all of Odeo's assets, Twitter included. He told TechCrunch the price was enough for the venture and angel investors to get their money back. He wanted, he wrote, a company without boards or investors' perceptions to worry about, and he admitted: "It may be stupid. It may be naive." Soon afterwards he fired Noah Glass, Odeo's co-founder and, by colleagues' accounts, Twitter's keenest early champion, who later said he felt betrayed.

Twitter took off at the South by Southwest festival in spring 2007, and a few months after the buyback Williams offered some old investors a chance to buy in at a $25 million valuation. Speaking to Business Insider in 2011, many still appreciated his gesture; one said it had been received as a gracious act. Others wondered how much he had known about Twitter's prospects, and the reporter concluded that this would probably never be known.

quote.text: And, which is yet worse, let every one but dive into his own bosom, and he will find his private wishes spring and his secret hopes grow up at another’s expense.
quote.locator: Book I, Chapter XXI, "That the profit of one man is the damage of another"
quote.translator: Charles Cotton (1685), ed. W. C. Hazlitt
quote.source_title: Essays of Michel de Montaigne — Complete, tr. Charles Cotton, Project Gutenberg eBook #3600
quote.connection: Montaigne says anyone who looks honestly inward will find hopes that grow at someone else's expense. Williams gave the investors their money back and also kept Twitter; whether his hopes for it already ran ahead of what he told them is the question the record leaves open.

reflection: Williams had money left and could have kept going for two more years. He chose to stop, say so in writing, and return the investors' money. He also kept the one piece he still believed in, and that is where the story becomes harder to judge.

When you step back from something, the people around you are owed the same clear account you give yourself, including the part you still hope for. You do not need to know how it will turn out. It is enough to say what you see and what you want, before anyone has to ask.
invitation: If you are winding down or changing a piece of work, write the two sentences you would send to the people involved: what is ending, and what you still hope for.

sources.title: Odeo Bought Back From Investors
sources.supports: Odeo announced in February 2005, raised $5 million led by Charles River Ventures, launched July 2005; faced dozens of competitors including iTunes; Williams had spoken publicly about mistakes; Obvious Corp bought Odeo's assets including Twitter; price undisclosed, Williams saying it was enough for the VCs and angels to be made whole and common shareholders to make a modest gain

sources.title: How Twitter Was Founded
sources.supports: Jack Dorsey's status idea presented in February 2006 by Glass, Dorsey and Florian Weber; Williams's September 2006 letter to investors (company going nowhere, felt bad, buy back shares so they would not take a loss) and its passage on Twitter ('much too early to tell what's there', fewer than 5,000 registered users); investors agreed and were made whole; Blaine Cook's recollection of a summer 2006 meeting on whether to turn Twitter off; Twitter's breakthrough at SXSW in spring 2007; offer to some investors at a $25 million valuation; firing of Noah Glass and his feeling of betrayal; investors' mixed views, including the 'gracious act' remark and doubts about what Williams knew

sources.title: I was wrong about Twitter
sources.supports: A reporter's recollection of interviewing Williams in November 2006: Williams bought back Odeo from its venture investors and renamed it the Obvious Corporation; he kept steering the conversation to Twitter, whose users then numbered in the thousands; Twitter later needed venture funding

cross_checks.claim: In October 2006 Williams's new company, Obvious Corp, bought all of Odeo's assets, including Twitter, from its investors
The investors, who had put about $5 million into Odeo, got their money back
At the time of the buyback Twitter had only a few thousand users
Williams had publicly admitted Odeo's mistakes before the buyback

research_notes: Price: never officially disclosed. Williams told TechCrunch (2006) it was enough for the VCs and angels to be made whole and the common shareholders to make a modest gain, and TechCrunch presumed a little over the $5 million raised; Business Insider (2011) says the amount was never reported but investors say they were made whole, and refers to a sale for approximately $5 million; Fortune (2013) says Williams bought Odeo back for $2 million. Williams wrote that Odeo still had plenty of money in the bank, which may explain the gap between the cash he put in and what investors received. The story says only that the price was enough for investors to get their money back, as Williams said. The letter is dated only to 'one day in September 2006' by Business Insider, which quotes part of it; the original letter is not public. Business Insider dates Apple's podcasting launch in iTunes to autumn 2005 (it was mid-2005), so the story gives no date for it. The reasons for Noah Glass's dismissal are disputed in Business Insider's reporting (clashing personalities, volatility, or his wish to run Twitter); the story reports only the firing and his own feeling of betrayal. Investors' doubts about what Williams knew are reported as theirs; there was no legal finding, and Business Insider's reporter concluded the question could not be settled. The slate named Williams, Stone and Dorsey; the decision was Williams's, Twitter began as Dorsey's idea, and Glass championed it, so all are credited. Fast Company's 2011 profile of Glass is blocked for the verifier and not cited; NBC News carries a syndicated copy of the Business Insider article, which is not counted as independent. Evhead.com no longer serves the 2006 post, so it is cited through the Internet Archive.
